newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian tycoon's rise shows business circle power.
newsitem.headline: Russian tycoon's rise shows business circle power.

text.p: The controversial rise of tycoon Boris Berezovsky from car dealer to Kremlin politician has highlighted and formalised the influence of powerful and wealthy business circles in Russian politics.

Berezovsky, the 50-year-old head of a financial empire which gives him a big say in the main Russian television channel ORT, was appointed deputy secretary of President Boris Yeltsin's influential Security Council on Tuesday.

In the uproar over his promotion, the opposition communists are seeking the head of Kremlin chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais, whom they accuse of being a "regent" and promoting his own allies while Yeltsin is off the scene awaiting heart surgery.
The communists are worried that Chubais is amassing power, but are also angered by the rise of one of Russia's most controversial businessmen.
Berezovsky, who keeps a low public profile, is widely thought to have been using his money and influence behind the scenes to help Chubais and Yeltsin.

"The active participation of ORT deputy general director Boris Berezovsky in the process of governing the state was no secret even for people who have only a passing interest in politics," the liberal newspaper Sevodnya said.
"The surprising thing was the official consecration of the civil marriage between Mr Berezovsky and the Kremlin."
The pro-communist Pravda-5 said Berezovsky's appointment showed that a "shadow government of top Russian businessmen" was no longer content to have influence behind the scenes.
"The bankers want more. They want to be sitting at the controls so they can steer the structures of power," it said.
Berezovsky, who has courted controversy throughout his career, has stayed predictably cool. He and Chubais have avoided comment on the criticism.

Ivan Rybkin, who has replaced Kremlin rebel Alexander Lebed in the post of the secretary of the Security Council, defended the appointment of Berezovsky in an interview with the commercial NTV television on Friday.
"It continues a number of appointments (to state posts) of wealthy people who have money of their own and a name in commercial circles," Rybkin said.
He gave as an example the appointment earlier this year of leading banker Vladimir Potanin to the post of first deputy prime minister in charge of economy.

Berezovsky's tasks are to include control over financial affairs involving breakaway Chechnya, Itar-Tass news agency said. No other details of his role on the advisory Security Council, grouping state and security officials, are known.

Berezovsky, a mathematician and associate member of Russia's prestigious Academy of Sciences, is a director of the LogoVAZ car producer and industrial giant which gives him a finger in many pies. He also owns a major stake in a bank.

As a director of ORT, which reaches most of Russia's 150 million people, he has presided over coverage which independent analysts say played a big role in Yeltsin's defeat of communist candidate Gennady Zyuganov in July's presidential election.
Just how far Berezovsky's influence goes is unclear.
Yeltsin's ousted confidant and personal security chief, Alexander Korzhakov, has accused Berezovsky of asking him to kill a business rival. Berezovsky denies the charge.
In 1994, his car was blown up in an apparent assassination attempt which he escaped unhurt, though his driver was killed.
Berezovsky and Chubais appear to have risen together.

Chubais, who was appointed Kremlin chief of staff after the election, masterminded Yeltsin's re-election and he has used his position to garner more power and influence as the president remains out of the Kremlin preparing for his heart operation.
